newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels say they have seized eastern Zairean city.
newsitem.headline: Rebels say they have seized eastern Zairean city.

text.p: Rebels said on Monday they had seized the eastern Zairean city of Goma as international relief agencies and policy planners focused on how to help more than one million Hutu refugees.

Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said in Geneva that "emergency lifelines" should be opened to help the refugees and displaced Zaireans alike, with corridors for the Hutus to return in safety to their homes in Rwanda and Burundi.
Fighting between Tutsi rebels and the Zairean army in eastern Zaire forced the evacuation on Saturday of the last foreign aid workers and left refugees without U.N. protectors.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Monday urged relief teams to return to rebel-held eastern Zaire to care for the refugees, who include armed Hutu fighters, sworn enemies of Tutsi forces.

"We give them security so that they can land and use the airport at Kilimba close to Uvira as well as in Goma, which is completely under our control," Kabila, who is not a Tutsi, said in an interview with the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).
Uvira, on the northern shore of Lake Tanganyika and south of Goma, was taken by the rebels more than a week ago and has been visited by a Reuters correspondent since its capture.
It was not possible to confirm independently the rebel claim to have seized all of the city of Goma, where fierce fighting over the weekend forced all international aid workers to flee.
Reuters correspondent Christian Jennings, in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi right next to Goma, said the border crossing was held by rebels on Monday and no fighting was heard all morning.
With much of eastern Zaire in chaos and information sketchy, it was too early to say how the proposed aid corridors for the refugees would work, aid workers said.
"I think we are really at the early stages of this...The exact definition of the organisation of this still has to be worked out," said Brenda Barton of the U.N. World Food Programme in Nairobi.
Aid workers said refugees had begun to move west from the world's largest refugee camp at Mugunga and deeper into Zaire.
An Organisation of African Unity peace mission opened talks with the Rwandan government in Kigali on Monday aimed at securing a ceasefire in eastern Zaire.
The OAU mission, led by assistant Secretary-General Anatole Tiendrebeogo, opened talks with Rwandan Prime Minister Pierre Rwigema, officials said.
In Brussels, the European Union said a ceasefire had to be declared before the flood of refugees and Zairean displaced caught in the two-week-old conflict could be helped on a mass scale.
"The essential first requirement is a ceasefire...Only then can we begin the massive humanitarian job that needs to be done," the EU's Irish presidency said in a statement on Sunday.

The violence has sent hundreds of thousands fleeing. The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said about 11,400 refugees, mostly Zaireans but including Rwandans, had arrived in southern Uganda. More than 10,000 had arrived in Burundi.

Ugandan security sources told U.N. officials that on Saturday and Sunday sporadic mortar attacks from Zairean territory hit areas of northwest Uganda where there are camps for Sudanese refugees. There were no reported casualties.

Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni has been a key backer of the Tutsis in Rwanda and diplomats said the mortar attacks, blamed on guerrilla groups fighting the Museveni government, seemed to be part of the broad conflict between the Zairean government and Tutsi rebels.
"It is the destabilisation of Uganda, to hammer Museveni," said one East Africa-based diplomat.
In a broadcast monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, Rwandan radio said the Rwandan government promised to help in all international efforts to end the conflict.
But the government statement accused the Kinshasa government and the international community of turning a blind eye to growing problems in the region for the past few months.

The statement went on to call on the international community to view the crisis in eastern Zaire as a conflict between the Zairean state and internal forces, rather than as a conflict between two countries.
Some two million Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing Tutsi reprisals after the genocide of up to a million Tutsis there.
"The further the refugees move west, the more difficult it will be for us to reach them. It may make repatriation and reconciliation impossible," UNHCR's Ogata said in a statement.
Bloody rivalry between majority Hutus and minority Tutsis has poisoned life in Rwanda and Burundi for generations and has now spilled on to the territory of vast, mineral-rich Zaire.
The crisis for Zaire has sharpened with the absence of veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, receiving treatment for cancer in Switzerland.

Zaire accuses Tutsi-led Rwanda, which has long complained of cross-border raids by Hutu hardliners living among the refugees, of sending troops to fight alongside the rebels. Journalists saw Rwandan troops in Goma on Saturday. Rwanda denies involvement.
